content: I personally ran the little experiment at the end of the FLT post to formalize Vinogradov’s three primes theorem using Prove2Me mentioned in the post. I'm going to use this thread to talk in more detail about the human experience of doing it.

What I did very concretely on the first day was:

  • I created a Project in my personal Claude Max 5x account with 50 words of prompt asking it to use Prove2Me to formalize the Hardy-Littlewood Circle Method. I picked the topic because I'd been fascinated with it after taking Akshay Venkatesh's Analytics Number theory class back in 2004, and spent the summer after attempting doing undergraduate research using it.
  • Claude talked me through making the 4 websites it wanted to use not blocked by the Project's default network restrictions, and made me an account on the site.
  • I then started a thread to work on formalizing the method. Claude picked the Weyl inequality, made a mission for ProveToMe to works towards it.
  • I then mostly only interacted with the agent to ask it to do work in parallel, since it wasn't going very fast but also my usage meter was not on track to using the "4 hour session" quota. I ended up setting up 6 threads to work on different lemmas. To my surprise, it finished Weyl's inequality on the first day this way, so I got more ambitious and set a new objective of getting all the way to Vinogradov's theorem.
  • It then drafted a bunch of lemmas and started working on it.

I probably spent 30 minutes of attention scattered through the day on this.
Are you saying it finished the proof? I would be interested to know exactly what can be done with this tool.

Yes! But not on the first day (Tuesday) when I started the experiment.

I ended up running out my personal plan quota on the Wednesday, with the progress being reducing Vinogradov's to Siegel–Walfisz.

So yesterday we had two other people point their personal Claude plans at the same problem on Prove2Me. (One asked to just work on the same problem, and it autonomously found my work to continue and made the second missing linked above. The other with something more like a "Help Tim Abbott on Prove2Me" as the prompt).

You can see the completed mission on Prove2Me here: https://prove2.me/missions/Multiplicative%20Number%20Theory%20I%3A%20Siegel%E2%80%93Walfisz%20and%20the%20Three%20Primes%20Theorem

I was very impressed with the fact that this worked.

I think one could likely do considerably more ambitious projects than this using Prove2Me, or a similar tool. But I would definitely do some optimizations for the process. The agents spent the majority of their time doing duplicate work, for example, because the overall setup didn't have them checking often for what others had completed. I'm sure this could be improved.
We used a mixture of Opus 5 and Fable 5.1; e.g. one of the folks just used Opus.

Tim Abbott said:

"this" being Vinagradov or FLT??

This here means Vinogradov. Basically, what I think is now possible is that if there's a dozen people who all want to formalize field X so that they can cheaply formalize and computer-verify new research in the area, it should be possible for one of them do upload a bunch of missions like this and people can contribute through pointing their agents at it.

Obviously one could use Prove2Me or any similar platform; the Lean code is of course portable between different proof databases. But Prove2Me was specifically designed to support agent collaboration, and I would imagine the easiest way to get a better version of it would be to contribute to the project itself.
I wonder how this compares to https://taucetiproject.github.io/TauCeti/ . I guess one data point is that apparently prove2me can prove FLT!
I think if we do end up with several platforms for doing this, I imagine the clever thing to do would be to have them sync their Lean proof databases with each other.

That looks like an outline and a formal statement. I can't find a link there to view / download a Lean project for the complete proof, where is it?

For that matter, the Prove2Me FAQ says "Every public theorem, definition, and proof is open for anyone to read, reuse, and import, and so is the agent harness itself." - but that doesn't come with any actual link (or any statement of what open source license is being used). Where can someone view and download the complete contents of Formalpedia and the code underlying Prove2Me?

At a glance, it seems like Prove2Me is mostly interested in scaling single-theorem formalization across multiple agents. TauCeti is more preoccupied with the systematic expansion of its own library. It would be great if we could find a way for Prove2Me proofs to be pitched as TauCeti PRs.

Yeah I think the Prove2Me website has some UI gaps around this. So you can download a Lean proof from Prove2Me using an agent, but I'm not sure their non-agent interface has a button for it.

I imagine this is the kind of thing they'll be thinking about adding now that the platform is better known.
The platform itself is quite new; e.g. here's the research paper for it: https://arxiv.org/html/2608.28433v1

I'd hope for a bulk download of the full set of definitions and proofs as a Lean project (or two such projects, one for each Lean version they're using). For example, automatically push all new definitions and proofs and changes to a GitHub repository. And link to that repository from the FAQ. Likewise for the source code to the platform itself.
Cf. Wikipedia where I can get to https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/Data_dumps within four clicks from the English Wikipedia home page (starting with "Developers" in the page footer).

In case it's interesting, I made a little visualization of this Circle Method collaboration using the same program that did the FLT visualization.

Obviously this is a far smaller experiment than FLT, but I think it really shows the potential for multiple people to collaborate on advancing the portion of the mathematics proof graph that is formalized in Lean, whether or not they are aware of each other.

The "community baseline" in the image were uploaded by a "Community Bot" account to Prove2Me from July 29-August 18. I'm not sure if that was an import from something like Tau˜Ceti or something else; I expect @Kunal Marwaha would know.

Visualization of the 3 primes

One thing you can see in the experiment is that a lot of statements were proven by more than one of the 3 accounts. So there's definitely some duplication of effort, which could surely be avoided with a fancier harness than all of the accounts working with the same database of statements, proof strategies, and proofs.

I think it would go a long way if you put the names of the members of your team on the documents you are generating.

Like, you could imagine a locking system where an agent can claim a given chunk of the unproved work, or can publish "I'm agent <UUID> and working on X". It does require some care though; agents that run out of quota do tend to stop suddenly.

One can also imagine not worrying about that too much.
I generated that document and I ran this little experiment, which as you can see on the visualization literally happened Tuesday=>Thursday of this week. What additional information would be helpful?

The point of this experiment was to determine whether one can do ambitious autoformalization work with a small number of people who just have a standard professional user AI plan, and point it at what they want to formalize using Prove2Me.

Having experienced this experiment, it is now my belief that projects similarly ambitious to Fermat's Last Theorem could be automatically formalized by a collaboration at a single math department, including drafting undergraduate students to help. I expect one would want some people running the project figuring out how to break up the work and orchestrate it, but once you've generated the graph, proving all the things in the graph is a naturally parallelizable problem; each theorem can be proved as "A,B,C,D,...K => Z", even if you've only proven A and G so far.

And most "mistakes" where resources are wasted, like using not the ideal definition of something, can probably be fixed after at the cost of proving equilvances or whatnot that make the resulting proof longer.

content:
It would take more logistics than it's probably worth to run this experiment again.

The proofs are already up on Prove2Me, so everything would show up in the "community baseline". But again, this small experiment used most of the weekly quota for 3 $100/month Max accounts. If you bought new subscriptions to do it, the cost would be 100 * 3 people / (4 weeks per month) ~= $75.

(And I imagine many researchers here either have existing plans or would be eligible for discounted plans from OpenAI and/or Anthropic's science programs.)

I think probably a lot of that can be back-computed using the proofs; your agent should be able to download the proofs from Prove2Me and compare them with the literature directly.

But my overall thesis is that there are lots of interesting ways to do this kind of experiment.

And my hope is that folks feel empowered to do their own rather than feeling like they need a gatekeeper to approve their experimental design.
The “Community Bot” account is run by one of the people who built prove2me.
